title: Stratified Analysis
text:
1. Consider Confounding and Effect Modification
Once you have identified food items associated with an elevated risk of becoming a case, the next step is to whether those associations are distorted or modified by a third variable.
Confounding and effect modification are two distinct phenomena, both involving a third variable, but leading to very different interpretation:

Confounding is a distortion of the observed association. The third variable is associated with both both the exposure and the outcome, and the crude estimate does not reflect the true effect (bias). When we stratify by the confounder, the stratum-specific estimates are similar to each other but differ from the crude estimate. We adjust for the confounding variable to control it.
Effect modification (aka interaction) is a real phenomenon: the effect of the exposure on the outcome genuinely differs across levels of the third variable. When we stratify, the stratum-specific estimates differ meaningfully from each other. Effect modification is not corrected because it is not a bias, it is described and reported openly.

We investigate both through stratification. For medium-to-large datasets, exploring variable by variable becomes impractical and we turn to regression methods. Here we will use csinter() from EpiStats to manually explore how the association varies across the levels of a third one.

Spanish tortilla as exposure of interest
Spanish tortilla came out second in RR during univariable analysis, suggesting a potential association between eating tortilla and becoming a case. A plausible explanation is that people who ate russian salad also ate Spanish tortilla, so the effect of tortilla is a simple reflection of the effect of russian salad (i.e., confounding). Alternatively, the tortilla effect could genuinely differ depending on whether russian salad was eaten (i.e., effect modification).
Stratification lets us distinguish between the two. The question is: does the association between Spanish tortilla and becoming a case hold once we account for the russian salad consumption?

## Stratified analysis between tortilla and becoming a case, by Russian salad consumption
csinter(x = clean, 
        cases = "case", 
        exposure = "spanish_tortilla", 
        by = "russian_salad")

$df1

When reading the output, compare:

The stratum-specific RRs to each other: if they differ meaningfully, suspect effect modification
The crude RR to the Mantel-Haenszel adjusted RR: if they differ substantially (rule of thumb for difference: > 10-20%) and the strata are homogeneous, suspect confounding.

Action — Is the relationship between Spanish tortilla and becoming a case confounded by the consumption of Russian salad?






CautionSee the solution





Step 1 — Any effect modification? Compare the two stratum-specific RRs:

Russian salad = 1 → RR = 1.58 (95% CI 0.91–2.75)
Russian salad = 0 → RR = 1.04 (95% CI 0.28–3.83)

Step 2 — Any confounding? Compare the crude and the adjusted RR:

Crude RR = 2.14 (95% CI 1.28–3.57)
MH-adjusted RR = 1.46 (95% CI 0.88–2.43)
Relative change = –31.83 %

A relative change above ~10–20 % is a common rule of thumb for meaningful confounding, and here it is roughly 32 %. The adjusted CI also crosses 1. So the apparent association between Spanish tortilla and becoming a case is largely explained by Russian salad consumption: once we account for who ate salad, tortilla no longer shows a clear independent effect.



Action — Check whether an association exists between eating Russian salad and Spanish tortilla. What implication does it have for assessing confounding or effect modification? Tip: you learned about the appropriate test a moment ago.






CautionSee the solution






# Chi-square test of association between two binary variables
chisq.test(clean$spanish_tortilla, clean$russian_salad)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  clean$spanish_tortilla and clean$russian_salad
X-squared = 16.173, df = 1, p-value = 5.78e-05


The Chi-squared test clearly identifies a correlation between the two food items, with a p-value of 5.78e-05 (0.0000578)
Why does this matter, and what should we see? For a variable to act as a confounder, it must satisfy three conditions:

Be associated with the exposure (here, Spanish tortilla).
Be associated with the outcome (here, becoming a case), independently of the exposure.
Not be on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.

This check addresses the condition 1. We know condition 2 from the univariable analysis, and condition 3 is plausible. If people who ate Russian salad were also much more likely to eat Spanish tortilla, then part of the crude “tortilla effect” we saw earlier was really the Russian salad effect leaking through — which is exactly the pattern of confounding we observed when the adjusted RR dropped from 2.14 to 1.46.





Optional: explore russian salad as the exposure of interest
Action — Conversely, is the association between Russian salad and becoming a case confounded by the consumption of Spanish tortilla? Discuss the result.






CautionSee the solution





Step 1 — Any effect modification? Compare the two stratum-specific RRs for Russian salad:

Spanish tortilla = 1 → RR = 4.91 (95% CI 1.65–14.59)
Spanish tortilla = 0 → RR = 3.21 (95% CI 1.30–7.93)

Woolf’s test gives p = 0.558, so there is no statistical evidence that the two RRs differ. Both are also well above 1 with CIs that exclude the null: the Russian salad effect is present and strong regardless of tortilla consumption.
Step 2 — Any confounding?

Crude RR = 4.39 (95% CI 2.28–8.44)
MH-adjusted RR = 4.05 (95% CI 1.97–8.32)
Relative change = –7.68 %

The adjusted estimate is almost identical to the crude one (change well below the ~10 % rule of thumb), and the CI remains far from 1. Spanish tortilla does not confound the Russian salad – case association.
Step 3 — Put the two stratified analyses side by side




Tortilla as exposure
Russian salad as exposure




Crude RR
2.14 (1.28–3.57)
4.39 (2.28–8.44)


MH-adjusted RR
1.46 (0.88–2.43)
4.05 (1.97–8.32)


Relative change (adj vs crude)
–31.8 %
–7.7 %


Adjusted CI crosses 1?
Yes
No



This asymmetry is the key diagnostic result of the stratified analysis:

The crude tortilla effect collapses when we account for Russian salad consumption → the association was largely explained by the fact that tortilla-eaters also tended to eat Russian salad.
The crude Russian salad effect persists almost unchanged when we account for tortilla consumption → Russian salad is associated with disease independently of tortilla.

Taken together, the evidence points to Russian salad as the likely vehicle of the outbreak, with Spanish tortilla acting as a “passenger” exposure whose apparent effect was confounded by salad consumption.

title: Univariate Analysis
section: 1. Factors associated with becoming a case
text:
1. Factors associated with becoming a case
You will start the analysis by exploring associations between some non-food variables and becoming a case. Several methods are available to you, but let’s explore the one you already now first, by using gtsummary::tbl_summary():
Action — Explore the non-food variables age, sex and group as the first step

Build a tbl_summary() stratified by case variable and include the add_p() call to perform a statistical comparison
Is any of the variables associated with becoming a case in our data?

Action — Can you identify the statistical test employed for each variable? Why would the Wilcoxon rank sum test be used here?






CautionSee the solution





# Perform statistical comparisson table using tbl_summary()
exp_agesexgroup_table <- clean %>% 
  select(case, age, sex, group) %>%   # variables of interest only
  mutate(case = recode_values(
  case,
  0 ~ "Non-case",
  1 ~ "Case")) %>% 
  tbl_summary(by = case) %>%          # stratifying variable
  add_p() %>%                         # perform statistical comparison
  bold_labels()                       # add some visuals

# see table
exp_agesexgroup_table
The Wilcoxon test was decided by tbl_summary() as it identified age to be non-normally distributed. You can also check it yourself with base r functions:
# Check if age overall follows a normal distribution:
shapiro.test(clean$age)

# Perform Wilcoxon rank sum test on age and sex:
wilcox.test(age ~ case, data = clean)

# Chi square test by hand, for demosntration
chisq.test(clean$sex, clean$case)
chisq.test(clean$group, clean$case)
Conclusion: age, sex and group were not significantly associated with becoming a case, i.e., we have not enough evidence to conclude that there was some differentiated exposure or behavior between attendees based on these characteristics. This can be interpreted like: they were all exposed to the same food items and showed no preference based on their age, sex or group

title: Univariate Analysis
text:
2. Risk associated with food exposure

Item by Item
To asses the relationship between the different food items and the risk of becoming a case, we will calculate risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals, food by food. For this, we will use the EpiStats package, one of the many existing libraries for epidemiology:
The CS() function builds the 2x2 table between an exposure and an outcome, that we declare as quoted arguments

# Calculate risk diffrence, risk ratios and attributable fraction among exposed
EpiStats::CS(clean,    # data
             "case",   # outcome variable, quoted
             "jamon")  # exposure variable, quoted

$df1
          Cases Non Cases Total Risk
Exposed      33        78   111 0.30
Unexposed    16        34    50 0.32
Total        49       112   161 0.30

$df2
                Point estimate 95%CI.ll 95%CI.ul
Risk difference          -0.02    -0.18     0.13
Risk ratio                0.93     0.57     1.52
Prev. frac. ex.           0.07    -0.52     0.43
Prev. frac. pop           0.05       NA       NA
chi2(1)                   0.08       NA       NA
Pr>chi2                  0.772       NA       NA


Action — Perform the univariate risk calculation over two other food items of your choice and interpret the results






ImportantInterpret the results of CS()





The outputs of CS()consist on two tables called $df1 and $df2 when printed in the console.
The first one is the 2x2 contingency table with exposed-unexposed and cases-non cases and the overall risk in each strata. For jamon, the risk of becoming a case was 30% for those who ate it, and 32% for those who didn’t.
The second table contain different risk estimators together with their 95% confidence interval:

Risk difference: is the crude difference between the risk of becoming a case in the exposed and the unexposed.
Risk ratio: relative measure of how higher or lower the risk among one group compared with the other.
Attributable fraction among the exposed and the population: proportion of the cases that can be explained with eating jamon.

We cannot establish the existence of an association between eating jamon and becoming a case.





All items at once (univariate)
You could also explore all food items at once with a single function to get a better overview in a single go, by creating a vector of food variables and passing it to the CSTable() function of the same EpiStats libraries:
# Food vector
food <- c("russian_salad", "spanish_tortilla", "jamon", "chicken",
          "watermelon", "wine", "water", "croquettes", "cheese")

# Risk ratio table for all food items
CSTable(clean, 
        "case", 
        food)    # vector of exposures
Action — Read and Interpret the results. Do you have any potential culprit hypothesis?
Optional — How would you turn the output from CSTable() into a ready-to-share table? Maybe you can use a bit of AI for this challenge.

title: Univariate Analysis
text:
3. Dose-response relationship
The questionnaire also included questions about the amount of each food item consumed, which gives us the chance of exploring whether a dose-response relationship exist. We will only explore russian_salad and spanish_tortilla as the only food items with increased risk.
You will use the library epitools with the function riskratio() because CS() can only handle binary (i.e., 2x2) tables, while dose-response include three categories already. The function works quite similarly:
# Calculate Risk Ratios by each consumption level, and associated p values
epitools::riskratio(clean$russian_saladD,                     
                    clean$case,                     
                    conf.level = 0.95)

epitools::riskratio(clean$spanish_tortillaD,                     
                    clean$case,                     
                    conf.level = 0.95)
Action — Can you affirm that a dose-response relationship exist for any of the two food items? How does it affect your overall hypotheses of association?

title: Case Definition
text:
1. Agree on a Case Definition
The Case Definition is a key step in any outbreak investigation. We need to agree on the conditions that a person needs to meet in order to be considered a case, i.e., not everyone attending the Family Day is by default exposed to the food vehicle, nor all symptomatic persons are sick.
Before continuing, stop and think about a plausible Case Definition for our outbreak. It’s always useful to start from the classical triad: place, persone and time:

Place: Does the mere fact of attending the Family Day qualify you as a potential case?
Person: Is everyone equally likely to become a case? Are all affected attendees cases by default?
Time: Every sick person is automatically considered a case?

Take a moment to think about them. Discuss with your colleagues and facilitators around if you’d like to. But most importantly for this exercise: how would the answer to those questions translate into your existing variables? Do you have all necessary information or you need to create new ones?






CautionSee the solution





After discussing, you finally reach the following Case Definition:

A Case is a person who:

Attended the Family Day at “Residencia Los Almendros” care home on Sept 13th
Ate from the lunch buffet
Became sick after eating (developed any symptoms)
Became sick within a defined time period of relevance (12-72h)


Other Case Definitions were possible, we just made a decision for this exercise. Sometimes you can develop multiple definitions to asses sensitivity and test its impact on the analyses, but that won’t the be the case today

title: Case Definition
text:
2. Who can be a Case?

Place criteria
Outbreaks linked to events or places may make you think the place criteria is not necessary. You ask for the attendance list and you have all potential exposed. But there is more to it when you examine the matter carefully.
Action — Do you have any variable that would make an attendee of the event disqualified to become a case? Think about the suspected transmission route of this outbreak
Action — What would you do with these persons? Can they stay in your study population?






CautionSee the solution





The variable buffet identifies attendees that also ate at the lunch buffet. If someone did not eat from there, the don’t have any chance of becoming a case, and therefore are not part of our study cohort and should be excluded:
# Filter away those who did not eat from the buffet
clean <- clean %>% 
  filter(buffet == "Yes")
Optional: take a quick look at those who did not eat from the buffet. In this case, they did not collect any further information through the questionnaire. But you’d be surprised about how many times they also report other information that may mislead you if you are not careful





Person criteria
Now we only have left those who attended the Family Day (i.e., are on the linelist) and ate from the buffet. Now you need to define who actually became sick. Since we don’t have any column that give you the information directly, we need to infer from the available symptoms.
Action — Create a new variable, gastro_symptoms, that becomes 1 for anyone reporting at least one of the five gastrointestinal symptoms, and 0 otherwise. Use case_when() for this task.






CautionSee the solution





# Filter away those who did not eat from the buffet
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(gastro_symptoms = case_when(
     # Use OR criteria to capture any of the symptoms as possitive condition
     diarrhoea == "Yes" | vomiting == "Yes" | 
       abdo == "Yes" | fever == "Yes" | 
       nausea == "Yes"    ~ 1,
     
     # If none of the above conditions are met, then
     .default = 0
    )
  )
Stop and think: Was including all gastro symptoms into our case definition the right choice? One should think that feeling a bit of abdominal pain, nausea, or even vomiting after eating in a buffet could mean only that you ate too much, for example. Those are very unspecific symptoms in terms of identifying potential cases given that we suspect something else going on. Once again, this is only an exercise, but always think about the consequences of your choices





Time criteria
If our hypothesis is that some consumed food was contaminated and caused an intoxication, then clinical symptoms should occur after the food was consumed. Not only that, disease should occur within a plausible time window that will later help us narrow down the potential causative agents, given their known incubation periods.

Define the onset day and time of sick people
For now, we have data on the day and hour of occurrence, but over two separated columns we need to merge together:
Action — Build a single onset_datetime from dayonset and starthour. For that, we have two potential options:

dmy_h(), a lubridate function where the “h” stands for “hour”, turns a character string into a date-time format. Useful if first you want to glue together both columns or modify the characters beforehand.
If both variables are already in <date> format, you can just add them together with + and voilà.







CautionSee the solution





# Create a date-time variable
clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(onset_datetime = dayonset + starthour)



Which path should you choose? For that, you would need to first check whether every onset day is also accompanied by an onset time. When you add them together, missing any of them will result in NA. What to do if some information is missing is also part of your decisions as epidemiologist. Do you want to assume some onset time, i.e. 00h? Do you exclude them from the time criteria? Do you restrict the time criteria to whole days? Think about it


Calculate incubation period in hours
The incubation period is the time elapsed between exposure to the causative agent and disease onset. It can be calculated in days or hours, depending on the pathogen and disease presentation. Since people became sick right after the buffet, hours seem like the logical choice:
Action — The buffet was served on September 13th at 14:00. Calculate the incubation variable, i.e. how many hours passed between the buffet and their symptom onset. For that:

Create a new date-time variable buffet_datetime using the adequate lubridate function.
Calculating the time period between any two dates can be as simple as calculating the difference between them using -, the subtraction symbol.
Convert this substraction to <numeric> class, as <difftime> is a specific variable type that can be problematic to handle.







CautionSee the solution





# Calculate the time span between two dates (Diffdate)
clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(buffet_datetime = ymd_h("2026-09-13 14h"),
         incubation = as.numeric(onset_datetime - buffet_datetime))



Optional — Explore the new incubation period variable. Can you find any strange values? We should now plot the incubation periods with a histogram to get an idea about our time criteria for deciding who is a case and who isn’t, developing symptoms between 12-72h post-buffet.






CautionSee the solution





Interpretation: among those developing symptoms, most of the report disease onset between 12 and 42 hours after eating the lunch buffet. Some people reported symptoms starting before the buffet, and also quite late >72h post-buffet.

clean %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = incubation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(clean$incubation, na.rm = T), 
                                  max(clean$incubation, na.rm = T), 
                                  12)
                     ) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Incubation Periods") +
  theme_bw()














3. Create the Case variable
Following the Case Definition we agreed upon, and after creating all needed variables, you are ready to create a new Case variable taking the value 1 for those meeting the case definition, and 0 otherwise
Action — Use case_when() to define your case variable using the person and time criteria

How many cases fulfill the Case Definition? 
What is the overall attack rate of this outbreak? 







CautionSee the solution






clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(case = case_when(
    # They experienced gastrointestinal symptoms
    gastro_symptoms == 1 & 
      
    # Symptom onset between 12 and 72h after eating at the buffet   
    incubation >= 12 & incubation <= 72   ~ 1,
    
    # Everything else
    .default = 0
  ))

# Count and Percentage of cases vs no cases
tabyl(clean$case)

 clean$case   n   percent
          0 118 0.7065868
          1  49 0.2934132

title: Data Import & Cleaning
text:
When starting a new task in R, you need to set up your workspace, folder structure and R Project before any other thing. Then, creating scripts, activating libraries and loading data will feel natural and smooth. You have practiced this already, but a refresher is always helpful:

Create a folder (or choose an existing one) to become your Project Folder 📂
Inside your project folder, create the recommended sub-folders for scripts, data, and outputs 📚
(that includes the raw and clean data folders, remember!)

Download the course’s data files and backups, extract them and store them accordingly

Open RStudio > New Project > Existing Directory > Create to set up your R Project 💼

Now you are truly set-up! Copy the exercise’s dataframes to the <raw> data folder to keep everything tidy and isolated.
Open a new script, and immediately save it in the <scripts> folder. You can name it 01_Data_Cleaning or something similar, to your own taste. It will become a good practice to number your scripts while clearly separating the different tasks you will perform within each of them.


Every script begins the same, there is no trick to it:

Activate libraries
Load data

The order here does matter, of course. Because you will need libraries to locate your files in the computer and read them to R automatically, right? Which libraries exactly should you activate first? You can start with something like this:
## Check wether pacman is installed and activate it or install and activate otherwise
if(!require("pacman")){install.packages(pacman)}

## Activate libraries with pacman
pacman::p_load(
  here,          # to create file paths
  rio,           # to import data
  janitor,       # tools for data cleaning and exploration
  gtsummary,     # for summary tables
  skimr,         # to explore dataframes  [NEW ONE]
  tidyverse,     # for data manipulation (always the last library!!!)
  
  update = T     # to make sure libraries are updated if new versions exist
)

## Import data using rio and here
raw <- import(here("data", "raw", "carehome_familyday_raw.csv"))
If you ask yourself which libraries should be activated at the very beginning, the answer is quite straightforward: rio, here and tidyverse. As you realize more libraries are needed later, you can always come back, write them up and execute p_load() as many time as needed - it’s free!
That is enough preparation, let’s dive in into exploring our data and planning the cleaning process

title: Data Import & Cleaning
text:
1. Explore the Data
When opening a new dataframe for the first time, you need to explore your variables with a general overview. Learn their class, their values or ranges, missingness, and identify the inconsistencies that need fixing. For that, you know already of functions like str(), glimpse() or summary().
Today I want to introduce to you a new library: skimr and its function skim(). It takes a dataframe as the main argument, and will provide you with an extensive overview of its variables. Let’s see this in action:
Action — Check the dimensions and structure of your raw data using skim(). Don’t assign this operation to any object, just let it print on the console and see.
The resulting output can be massive: overall information like rows, cols, number of variable per type and then a fine-grained description of variables grouped by their type, with adequate information for each, especially character/numeric ones. Answer this question just from the skim() output:
How many rows does raw has? 
How many numeric variables are present? 
How many entries are missing information on consumed food? 
How many unique identifiers (id) are present? 
How many entries has missing onset day info? 
And how many has information on onset day? 
How many entries has missing hour of symptom start? 
You see - there is a lot you can learn from your data with a single function call
Action — Would you clean variables names?
Action — Do you spot something odd that warrants further investigation for cleaning? Can you think of the needed transformations that are required?






TipHint - Most common cleaning needs





Among the very first things you should check for any dataframe is variable class, and its implications. Numeric variables coded as character, or viceversa. Dates as characters. Characters that should have an order - factors.
The other key issue is about extreme or implausible values for your variables. This will depend on every variable, of course, but a classical one are age values. Also, don’t forget categories within character values. All of them should be explored before running into any further analysis.









CautionSee the solution





Below you can find one possible solution for exploring variables. You may use different functions or approaches, because you already know a few of them. As long as you are able to understand your data and spot cleaning needs, that’s perfectly fine.
## Dataframe summary
skimr::skim(raw)

## Further exploring
range(raw$age)  # see min and max values of a numeric vector

unique(raw$sex)      # Main present categories with unique
unique(raw$group)
unique(raw$buffet)

tabyl(raw$vomiting)    # check some symptoms and fodd item variables with tabyl
tabyl(raw$croquettes)
tabyl(raw$croquettesD)
After exploring the data, you should have realized at least three things requiring cleaning:

age: some obviously implausible values are present and we need to decide whether they can be fixed, turned into NAs or deleted
dates: we have two of them that require transformation - and potentially a merge
categories as numbers: practically all symptoms and food item variables were read as numbers because they are coded as 0-1. We should fix that turning them into factors

title: Data Import & Cleaning
text:
2. Data Cleaning

Fixing age
Look at the range of age: some values are clearly impossible, and likely represent typos or writing mistakes. Decide, for each implausible value, whether it’s an obvious typo you can confidently correct, or one you can’t.
Action — Tables are more than outputs for other people. They assist you during your work. For example, try to cross-tabulate age and group to find about about the nature of the mistakes, and get inspired about potential solutions.
Action — Clean accordingly to the previous step using case_when() and the adequate conditions so only the affected rows are modified. Start working on a new object named clean. Would you apply the same fix when the same implausible value affects a resident and a family member?






CautionSee the solution





# Crosstabulate age and group using janitor to find inplausible values
raw %>% tabyl(age, group)

# Fix the age variable whit case_when()
clean <- raw %>% 
  mutate(age = case_when(
    # negative age value to positive
    age == -35  ~ 35, 
    # if 190 years and family member, assume 19 years typo
    age == 190 & group == "family"  ~ 19, 
    # if 190 years and resident, assume 90 years typo
    age == 190 & group == "resident"  ~ 90,
    # everyone else stays the same
    .default = age
  ))
Not every bad value has an obvious fix. A rule like “correct it if the error is unambiguous (an extra digit, a stray minus sign); set it to NA if you’d just be guessing” is a defensible, explicit policy - and one you can state in a line of code, not just in your head.
Hadn’t you cross-tabulated by group first, relying only on the age range, your fixing may have looked different. Use the information available whenever possible.





Fixing dates
We learned about working with dates using lubridate and how the available functions are chose based on our date variable structure, e.g. year-month-day for a “2026-09-13” date. Even if our date variable is in text format, the same logic remains. But what to do with the starthour variable? Once again, lubridate is prepared to handle that with an hours() function
Action — Change the variable class of dayonset and starthour to <date> format using lubridate. Include it in your clean object you started before






CautionSee the solution





You can include this cleaning step by either updating the clean object from the previous step or by adding it with a pipe in the first cleaning chain starting with raw.
# Update the clean object from before
clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(
    dayonset = dmy(dayonset),
    starthour = hours(starthour)
  ) 


# Or add a new pipe to your cleaning chain
clean <- raw %>% 
  mutate(age = case_when(
    # negative age value to positive
    age == -35  ~ 35, 
    # if 190 years and family member, assume 19 years typo
    age == 190 & group == "family"  ~ 19, 
    # if 190 years and resident, assume 90 years typo
    age == 190 & group == "resident"  ~ 90,
    # everyone else stays the same
    .default = age
  )) %>% 
  # Fix dates format
  mutate(
    dayonset = dmy(dayonset),
    starthour = hours(starthour)
  ) 





Fixing symptoms and food variables
Interestingly, we have a fair number of columns that are coded the same:

Symptoms and Food are binary 0-1 (yes or no) columns
FoodD columns indicate the amount of the consumed food, all of them range between 0 (no or very little consumption) to 3 (more than 1 piece)

Fixing them one by one inside a massive mutate is possible, sure. But also extremely boring, problematic and subject to writing typos because of repetition. We can do better using the Tidyverse helper function across(), that facilitates applying the same transformation to multiple columns at once inside mutate()and summarise() calls.
It works by specifying a set of columns and the function to apply to all of them, like this:
clean <- raw %>% 
  mutate(across(                           # direct call without a name
    .cols = c(var1, var2, var5, var14),    # set of variables to modify
    .fns = ~ as.character(.)    # we use a tilde (~) to declare the function
  ))                            # and a point (.) to indicate data from .cols
To declare the columns to modify, you can use more helper functions that answer to the question “Which of the existing variables are picked?”. The answer can be: “all of these variables”, “only those of class character”, “those that begin with the character ‘date_’”, “those that has a letter ”D” at the end of their name”… and so on [pure grammar model, isn’t it?]

Change all variables inside a vector
To begin with, we create a vector binary_cols that contains the name of all the binary 0-1 variables in our data we want to change:
binary_cols <- c("diarrhoea", "vomiting", "abdo", "fever", "nausea",
                 "buffet")
Now we will use the selecting function all_of() to declare the columns to modify inside across(). The function to apply will be factor() over all of them. Remember to include the arguments levelsand labels to indicate 0 = “No” and 1 = “Yes”
Action — Convert all of the binary variables to labelled factors (“No”/“Yes”) in one step.






CautionSee the solution





clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(across(
    # Transform all variables in the binary_cols vector
    .cols = all_of(binary_cols),
    # By transforming then into 0-1 factors with "No"-"Yes" labels
    # Base R version of transforming into factor
    .fns = ~ factor(., 
                    levels = c(0, 1),
                    labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  ))

#check
class(clean$diarrhoea)





Change food dose using a name pattern
For the food-dose variables, we can take advantage of the way they were named as they always include a final capital “D”. The helper function ends_with() becomes useful for this:
clean <- clean %>% 
  mutate(across(
    .cols = ends_with("D", ignore.case = FALSE),
    # Tidyverse version to convert into factor
    .fns = ~ as_factor(.)  
  ))

#check
class(clean$croquettesD)
The added the ignore.case argument to FALSE to force the function to differentiate between capital “D” and any d (default behavior). Because this time we were not interested in adding labels to the factor, we could rely on the tidyverse as_factor() function.
Action — Add the food-dose variable mutate to the cleaning pipe or update the clean object to keep the changes

title: Data Import & Cleaning
section: Save and Export the cleaned dataframe
text:
Save and Export the cleaned dataframe
With these cleaning steps we can now save a new dataframe to continue working from it. Use the export() function with here() to define the path and filename. Because we created factors, the only format we can use is the R native format .rds
Action — Save the cleaned dataframe as carehome_clean1.rds in the clean data folder
export(clean, here("data", "clean", "carehome_clean1.rds"))

title: Descriptive Analyses & Laboratory Data
text:
For this exercise, you should continue right after Case Definition, with a dataset containing the variable case with the adequate number of cases (49). To make things easier, you have a second backup file containing the right data to continue working error-free: carehome_clean2.rds

Start a fresh new script for descriptive analysis, give it the name you prefer, but make it self-explanatory and number preferably
Like always, you will first activate your libraries and load your data. Today, in addition to the cleaned backup data, you will load the lab data containing microbiological results of the patient’s samples. Load it at the beginning as well:

## Check wether pacman is installed and activate it or install and activate otherwise
if(!require("pacman")){install.packages(pacman)}

## Activate libraries with pacman
pacman::p_load(
  here,          # to create file paths
  rio,           # to import data
  janitor,       # tools for data cleaning and exploration
  flextable,     # for formatting tables
  gtsummary,     # for summary tables
  skimr,         # to explore dataframes  [NEW ONE]
  tidyverse,     # for data manipulation (always the last library!!!)
  
  update = T     # to make sure libraries are updated if new versions exist
)

## Import clean data using rio and here
clean <- import(here("data", "backup", "carehome_clean2.rds"), trust = T)
lab <- import(here("data", "raw", "carehome_familyday_lab.csv"))

title: Descriptive Analyses & Laboratory Data
text:
1. Descriptive analyses
Description of the sample should follow the same logic of person-place-time that we used for the case definition. But this time, we already defined who is a considered a case and who is not, so we will explore the characteristics that will lead us later to further analyses in the next investigation steps.

Person: Attack Proportions
We will start with the basics: counts and percentages.
Action — What is the overall Attack Proportion? What function can you use to quickly answer this, without worrying too much about sharing any output.

What is the overall Attack Proportion of this outbreak? 

Action — Create a summary table with tbl_summary() exploring the distribution of age, sex and group among cases and non-cases. Answer the following questions with the basic table for now:

What is the Attack Proportion among females? 
What is the Attack Proportion among residents? 
What is the Median age of all attendees to the Family Day? 

Action — Use the code below to produce a single summary table, enhanced and ready-to-export to Word:






CautionReady-to-export table, ready-to-reuse code





The code below notably improves the tbl_summary() output. It is also a more complex code that includes html and markdown notation using a glue approach. There is a chance none of those words were even familiar for you. And that’s ok, you don’t need to understand it right now.
What you need to understand is that, by copying this code, you can adapt it to all your future tables only by changing the name and amount of labels and headers, and that is valuable
## Quick way to see the percentage of cases among the total participants
janitor::tabyl(clean, case)

## Complete Table Summary of Age, Sex and Group counts by Case status
table1 <- clean %>% 
  # only columns of interest
  select(case, age, sex, group) %>% 
  mutate(case = recode_values( # We recode case so that the table is easier to understand
  case,
  0 ~ "Non-case",
  1 ~ "Case"
)) %>% 
  tbl_summary(by = case,                 
              # modify row headers to make them prettier/easier to understand
              label = list(
                age ~ "Age",            
                sex ~ "Sex", 
                group ~ "Group"
              )) %>% 
  bold_labels() %>%                      
  # add total column
  add_overall() %>% 
  # customize header labels and appearance
  modify_header(
    #Text in the upper left corner ( ** make the text bold )
    label = "**Characteristic**"
  ) 

# Export to Word using flextable
table1 %>% 
  as_flex_table() %>% 
  autofit() %>% 
  save_as_docx(path = here("outputs", "Table_1.docx"))





Person: Age and Sex Distribution
We know about the median ages and sex distribution of cases and non-cases, but we should explore further to find potential differences for example between residents of the care home and their families. We can do that with both a table and a boxplot:
Action — Cross-tabulate age and sex by group using tbl_summary(). Don’t worry about exporting this one.
Action — Build a boxplot (or violin plot) of age by group to illustrate the finding of the table. For now, just include a single pre-defined theme as the only visual enhancement, don’t worry about further customization.






CautionSee the solution





# Table with Age and Sex distribution among residents and family members
clean %>% 
  select(group, age, sex) %>% 
  tbl_summary(by = group)

# Violin plot of age among residentes and family members
clean %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = age)) +
  geom_violin() +
  theme_bw()





Person: Symptoms by Case Definition
Action — Produce a summary table displaying the symptoms among cases and non-cases. Probably you can recycle the vector you created to clean these columns for this task. Which symptom was the more common among cases?
⭐ Extra! — Create a bar-plot of symptom’s frequency among cases (only if you have time later on)






CautionSee the solution





# Create a vector with the symptoms variables
symptoms <- c("diarrhoea","vomiting","abdo","fever","nausea")

# Table summary of symptom distribution by case definition
clean %>% 
  select(all_of(symptoms), case) %>% 
  tbl_summary(by = case) %>% 
  bold_labels() %>% 
  italicize_labels()

# Barplot of symptom distribution among cases
clean %>% 
  select(symptoms, case) %>% 
  # we need to pivot to long format for the counts
  pivot_longer(
    all_of(symptoms),  
    names_to = "symptom",
    values_to = "present"
  ) %>% 
  # only interested in symptoms among cases
  filter(present == "Yes", 
         case == 1) %>%    
  # Start of the graph
  ggplot(aes(
    # this trick arranges categories by frequency automatically 
    y = fct_infreq(symptom))
    ) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkred",   # some aesthetics
           alpha = 0.70) +
  labs(x = "Number of cases",  # custom labels
       y = "") +
  # predefined theme, as always
  theme_minimal()





Place: nothing to explore for now
Because we are in the context of a single event, place is already accounted with all included attendees. In this particular outbreak, we did not collect any other information that could have impacted the outbreak in terms of place like table distribution, serving times, or attending personnel. All those could constitute elements of place, even if not that straightforward.


Time: Epicurve of Cases
You explored the incubation period distribution to decide about the Case Definition time criteria. Now we have our cases and we should aim to building the outbreak’s epicurve using the onset_datetime we created:
Action — Create the epicurve only for cases and using scale_x_datetime() to add 6h breaks
Action — Reflect on the difference between the histogram of incubation times we plotted previously and this epicurve






CautionSee the solution





# Epicurve with datetime customization
clean %>%  
  # Only cases
  filter(case == 1) %>% 
  # Add onset_datetime to ggplot aesthetic:
  ggplot(aes(x = onset_datetime)) + 
  #Add histogram layer
  geom_histogram() +
  # select 6h breaks with custom date-time labels
  scale_x_datetime(
    date_breaks = "6 hours",
    date_labels =  "%d %b\n%H:%M") +
  # Update x and y axis labels
  labs(x = "Date and time of symptoms onset", 
       y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_bw()

title: Descriptive Analyses & Laboratory Data
text:
2. Joining lab results
The lab dataframe contains 66 entries with sample_dates and salmonella_results, the only positive result among all tested GI pathogens. The results are linked to the same patient id recorded in the cohort dataframe. You learned about joins quite recently, so take a look if you don’t remember about it:
Action — Perform the join of the lab results. What happened to the row with no lab results at all?
Action — Cross-tabulate case against salmonella_result. How would you interpret these results?






CautionSee the solution





# Simple left join of lab data by person's id
clean <- clean %>% 
  left_join(lab, 
            by = "id")

# Cross-tabulation of case and lab result
clean %>% 
  tabyl(case, salmonella_result)
Not every case has a positive test result. That is perfectly fine and common, as microbiology sampling is subject to limitations such as the time elapsed from clinical onset until collection, sensitivity, and other limitating factors. In this outbreak, laboratory confirmation was not part of the Case Definition and, therefore, this information remains confirmatory of the causative agent of the outbreak.
